{{Short description|Scottish mathematician and astronomer}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2018}}
{{Use British English|date=February 2018}}

'''David Gibb''' [[FRSE]] (31 October 1883 – 28 March 1946) was a Scottish mathematician and astronomer. He was the first person to use the term ''[[numerical integration]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://jeff560.tripod.com/q.html|title=Earliest Known Uses of Some of the Words of Mathematics (Q)|website=jeff560.tripod.com|access-date=2018-05-13}}</ref>

==Life==
Gibb, eldest son of Robert Gibb, a salt manufacturer, and his wife Joanna, was born in [[Methil]] near [[Leven, Fife]] on 31 October 1883. He attended Leven Public School and then [[George Watsons College]] in [[Edinburgh]] (1896–99). He studied mathematics and sciences at the [[University of Edinburgh]], graduating  with a MA/BSc in 1906 . While being a student, he lodged with Mr Flockhart at 3 West Preston Street, Edinburgh. In 1909 he began lecturing in mathematics at the university.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/Gibb.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150921180232/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/Gibb.html|archive-date = 21 September 2015|title = David Gibb - Biography}}</ref>

In 1910 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] for his contributions to mathematics and astronomy. His proposers were [[George Chrystal]], Sir [[Frank Watson Dyson]], [[Cargill Gilston Knott]] and [[Ellice Horsburgh]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=1 July 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

During the [[First World War]] he worked on the Ballistic Department Ordnance Committee at the [[Royal Arsenal]] in [[Woolwich]], remotely calculating complex gun angles to fire on hidden or obscured targets, such as at the Gallipoli peninsula.<ref>Edinburgh Mathematical Society, obituary, March 1946</ref>

He returned to the University of Edinburgh after the war. From 1920 he had been President of the [[Edinburgh Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/ems/booklet.html |title=EMS 125th Anniversary booklet |website=www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk |access-date=14 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090421202021/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/ems/booklet.html |archive-date=21 April 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1934 he was promoted to Reader in Mathematics and remained in this role until his death in 1946. He died in [[Edinburgh]] on 28 March 1946.<ref>The Scotsman (newspaper) 30 March 1946</ref>

==Publications==

*''A Course in Interpolation and Numeric Integration for the Mathematical Laboratory'' (1915)
